This repo is the source repository for GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents. Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

day.description: Use your most capable model to audit your codebase and write plans for cheaper models to execute.
day.readme: An agent skill that audits any codebase and writes implementation plans for other agents to execute. The idea: use your most capable model for the part where intelligence compounds, understanding the codebase, judging what's worth doing, writing the spec, and hand execution to cheaper models. The skill never implements anything itself. The plan is the product. Works in any agent that supports Agent Skills format. The plans it writes are plain markdown, so any agent (or human) can pick them up.

day.description: Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents.
day.readme: Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents. Skills encode the workflows, quality gates, and best practices that senior engineers use when building software. These ones are packaged so AI agents follow them consistently across every phase of development. 9 slash commands that map to the development lifecycle. Each one activates the right skills automatically. In Claude Code these install as plugin commands.

day.description: Browser automation CLI for AI agents
day.readme: Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call.

week.description: Auto Ontology is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data. It enables deterministic query generation, better context retrieval, and more explainable AI for LLM and agent workflows.
week.readme: Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API.

week.description: Computer use CLI for AI agents
week.readme: Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree. agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library.

week.readme: My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding. Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve. Scrape static pages, render JavaScript, interact with websites, and extract data from the API calls behind them. new.description: Emulate macOS on iOS and iPadOS
new.readme: Download macOS, install it on the device, and use it. Own emulator, iOS gives apps no hypervisor, so Henge runs the Mac's arm64 code through its own JIT, with its own MMU and devices. It doesn't use QEMU or Virtualization.framework. Installs on the device, Henge downloads Apple's restore image and restores it the way a Mac does. No Mac needed, and nothing is decrypted or patched. Graphics, macOS draws through a virtual GPU, and Henge replays its commands with Metal.

Just sitting there, in a personal computer, being personal. You may have thought of this as "a computer working normally". On a recent episode of Cheeky Pint, the CEO of OpenAI offered another view: That RAM, he added, is "being used maybe 5% of the time".

new.description: 3D modeling in Python, built for LLMs.
new.readme: 3D modeling in Python, built for LLMs. sand3d is a Python library for writing 3D objects as short programs: profiles, solids, edits, frames, joints and assemblies, over Blender's bpy. A program says how a shape is made, part by part and in its own words, so a model writes it in a few hundred tokens How it is measured, part by part Short. A part takes 2 to 6× fewer tokens than the same part in Blender Python, CadQuery or FeatureScript (details). The whole API fits in a prompt, about 3,600 tokens (the API).

new.description: A GPU task manager for Windows, Linux, and WSL: per-process VRAM, GPU activity, and LLM model/KV-cache insights (Windows AMD and NVIDIA).
new.readme: An htop for what's inside your GPU, not just how full it is. Windows + NVIDIA/AMD, with Linux and WSL support (NVIDIA everywhere, AMD and Intel on native Linux; see Linux and WSL) and macOS on Apple Silicon (see macOS). A terminal UI that connects per-process GPU memory and engine activity with loaded runtimes, model files, and Task Manager says "15 GB used." This tries to answer: by what? Model weights? KV cache? Your browser? The desktop compositor? And why is so much GPU memory in system RAM?

new.description: A small, fast container runtime for macOS, Windows and Linux
new.readme: A tiny, fast container runtime for macOS, Windows and Linux. Runs your Docker images and works with the docker CLI, Compose and buildx you already use. items.title: Agencies self-host image generation and keep a cheap vision model as a quality gate
items.connection: MiniMax H3-Image open weights let teams generate images on their own hardware, and Liquid AI's 2B vision-language model cheaply captions or checks images, so generation and automated review run on the same box.
items.context: per-image API fees add up fast for creative agencies at volume
chain: Open H3-Image weights move text-to-image off metered APIs onto owned hardware.
A 2B vision model is cheap enough to describe or score every generated image.
The agency builds a loop that auto-rejects off-brief or malformed outputs before a human sees them.
Cost per usable image falls and reviewer time shifts to the good candidates.
items.who: Creative and marketing agencies benefit; the studio owner pays for hardware once.
items.versus: Pay-per-image APIs charge for rejects too and keep review manual; self-hosting plus an auto-check pays hardware once and filters free.
items.smallest_test: Generate 500 images locally, auto-caption with the 2B model, auto-flag mismatches against the brief; success if the flag agrees with a human reviewer on at least 80% of rejects.
items.disconfirm: The small vision model's captions are too noisy to separate good from bad, so humans still review everything.

items.title: Agent-built front ends get smaller and portable across coding harnesses at once
items.connection: Chrome guidance steers agents toward native browser primitives, and pstack workflows already translate across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and others, so the guidance can ride into many harnesses as a shared workflow.
items.context: teams often standardize on more than one coding harness across projects
chain: Chrome guidance makes agents default to CSS.highlights, showModal and field-sizing instead of heavy JavaScript.
pstack gives a vehicle that carries one workflow across several harnesses.
A team encodes the web-primitives guidance once and applies it everywhere its agents run.
Front-end output shrinks and dependency counts fall consistently, not just in one tool.
items.who: Front-end and platform teams benefit; the eng lead who owns tooling pays.
items.variable: JavaScript bundle size per generated page
items.versus: Hand-tuning each harness separately is slow; one translated workflow applies the guidance uniformly.
items.smallest_test: Encode the guidance as a pstack workflow, generate the same component in two harnesses, compare bundle size and dependency count to baseline; success if both shrink by a meaningful margin with equal function.
items.disconfirm: Agents ignore the guidance, or output differs so much across harnesses that one workflow cannot steer them.

items.title: AWS teams reuse one cached plan so cheap models execute large refactors
items.connection: shadcn/improve splits work into a plan written once by a strong model, and Kimi K3.1 Pro on Bedrock offers explicit prompt caching, so the shared plan becomes a cached prefix every executor call reuses.
items.context: cached prompt prefixes are usually billed well below fresh input tokens
chain: A strong model audits the codebase and writes one detailed plan.
Many executor calls each send the same plan plus one task, the exact shape explicit caching rewards.
Kimi on Bedrock runs those calls at a cached rate, so the dominant token cost is paid once instead of per task.
A team already locked into AWS cuts spend on big migrations without new vendor contracts.
items.who: Engineering teams on AWS benefit; the CTO or platform budget pays.
items.versus: Buying a premium coding seat pays full price on every execution token; this reuses the plan as a cache.
items.smallest_test: Run one multi-file refactor with a strong planner and Kimi executors using prompt caching, measure token bill versus doing the whole job on the strong model; success if cost drops at least 40% with comparable diff quality.
items.disconfirm: Cached execution produces worse diffs that need rework, erasing the savings.

items.title: Scriptable security review in CI gets a graded human gate for routine fixes
items.connection: OpenAI's Codex Security CLI finds, validates and fixes vulnerabilities from CI, and Kiro's Approve for Me grades which actions run automatically, so low-risk fixes can land while risky ones wait for a person.
items.context: security backlogs stall because every fix waits on scarce reviewer attention
chain: A scriptable security agent slots into the review pipeline and proposes validated fixes.
Graded permissions let routine, low-risk fixes proceed automatically and hold risky ones for review.
Reviewers only see the fixes that actually need judgment.
A small team clears more of its vulnerability backlog without hiring and without blanket auto-merge.
items.who: Small and mid-size engineering teams benefit; the security lead or eng manager pays.
items.variable: validated fixes merged per reviewer hour
items.versus: A security CLI alone still queues every fix for a human; adding a graded gate releases the safe ones.
items.smallest_test: Run the Codex Security CLI on one repo, route its fixes through a graded approval rule, track a month; success if routine fixes merge automatically with zero reviewer-reverted regressions.
items.disconfirm: The agent's false positives or unsafe fixes force reviewers to inspect everything anyway.

items.title: Browser apps ship private on-device image models with per-user LoRA tuning
items.connection: ExecuTorch WebGPU runs exported PyTorch models in Chrome and Safari with on-device LoRA, and Unsloth trains diffusion models locally, so one pipeline trains then ships a model that never leaves the browser.
items.context: many firms cannot send user content to third-party inference APIs
chain: Unsloth handles the heavy local training or fine-tune of a model.
torch.export produces one .pte file that runs the same in Chrome and Safari client side.
On-device LoRA lets each user personalize without uploading their data.
A privacy-sensitive product offers personalization with no server inference cost and no data egress.
items.who: Privacy-focused consumer apps and regulated-sector tools benefit; the product team pays to build the pipeline.
items.variable: server inference cost per active user
items.versus: Hosted inference costs per request and raises data-handling questions; this moves both to the user's device.
items.smallest_test: Export one small model, run it in both browsers, apply a LoRA on-device to a user sample; success if it runs on a mid-range laptop and personalization visibly improves output.
items.disconfirm: The exported model is too slow or large to run acceptably on common browser hardware.
